title: Lawyering and justice in a world that we know is riven by injustice
author: Emily Newburger

dom.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards

st.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central claim that broader entry and diversity commitments have not eliminated unequal professional rewards. It documents the stark underrepresentation of Black women in partnerships and the federal judiciary despite their substantial share of Black law graduates, while treating post-2020 institutional pledges as responses to persistent inequality rather than proven remedies.
qs: Even though they constitute more than 50% of all Black law students and Black law school graduates since the 1990s, they constitute less than 1% of all partners and less than 2% of the federal judiciary.

kp.k: Black representation increased without proportionate professional power
kp.d: Reporting David Wilkins’s late February talk, the March 22, 2022 article describes growth from approximately 2,200 Black lawyers in 1960 to approximately 65,000 at the time of the talk. Wilkins nevertheless says Black lawyers account for less than 5% of the bar, with still lower representation in positions of power and prestige. These are reported historical and contemporary claims, not findings about AI.
qs: The good news, he said, is there are now 65,000 or so Black lawyers in the United States. In 1960, there were something like 2,200 Black lawyers in the entire country.
But currently, Black lawyers account for less than 5% of members of the bar. And when you look at positions of power and prestige in the legal profession, he said, that number is lower.

kp.k: Black women face particularly persistent advancement barriers
kp.d: Wilkins contrasts Black women’s majority share of Black law students and graduates since the 1990s with their limited representation among all partners and federal judges. The comparison distinguishes educational participation from access to professional leadership.
qs: Even though they constitute more than 50% of all Black law students and Black law school graduates since the 1990s, they constitute less than 1% of all partners and less than 2% of the federal judiciary.

kp.k: Most Black lawyers serve individuals and small businesses
kp.d: Wilkins argues that most Black lawyers lack opportunities to become law-firm partners or federal judges. He characterizes their work and earnings through a historical comparison with Thurgood Marshall’s representation of Black individuals and small businesses in the 1930s.
qs: And most Black lawyers don’t have a chance to become partners of law firms or to become federal judges, said Wilkins.
“Most of them work in a manner and earn comparable wages to what Thurgood Marshall did in the 1930s by representing Black individuals and small Black businesses.”

kp.k: Access to justice remains racially unequal
kp.d: Wilkins places unequal access to justice alongside disparities in income, wealth and opportunity. He says events since 2020 accentuated these divisions, beginning with COVID’s disproportionate effects on communities of color.
qs: But Black Americans lag behind white Americans in almost every category of opportunity, he added, including income, wealth — and access to justice.
And events since 2020 have only accentuated this divide, beginning with the disproportionate effects of COVID on communities of color, he said.

kp.k: Educational inclusion enables institutional racial-justice initiatives
kp.d: Wilkins attributes an important role in corporate and law-firm racial-justice initiatives to Black lawyers who gained authority through expanded educational opportunity. He explicitly acknowledges other contributors. As an example, the article describes Kenneth Chenault and Kenneth Frazier’s OneTen initiative and its prospective goal of recruiting companies to create more than one million jobs for Black inner-city workers within 10 years; this is an initiative’s objective, not an achieved outcome.
qs: When you ask, what are the ripple effects of affirmative action, diversity and inclusion in higher education, we see these effects by these initiatives, which are not, of course, solely because of Black lawyers or even Black individuals.
There are many people who have contributed.
But I can guarantee that you will find at every company, at every law firm, Black lawyers who have pushed these initiatives.
which is recruiting companies to create more than one million new jobs for Black inner-city workers within the next 10 years.

kp.k: Growing Black power encounters backlash and credibility challenges
kp.d: Wilkins identifies backlash against growing Black political and economic power, citing race-conscious admissions litigation and attacks on the credentials and objectivity of Biden’s promised Black female Supreme Court nominee before a selection was announced. He connects those attacks to earlier challenges to Thurgood Marshall and other Black federal judges.
qs: This growing Black political and economic power has also generated backlash, said Wilkins, citing the race-conscious college admissions case to be heard before the Supreme Court next year.
Wilkins described the way even a hypothetical Black female nominee’s credentials and objectivity were being questioned prospectively.
These attacks are not new, said Wilkins, noting they were made against Thurgood Marshall when he was nominated to the Supreme Court and against other Black judges selected for the federal bench.

kp.k: Professional identity cannot be separated from personal identity
kp.d: Wilkins describes, but rejects, the traditional conception that professional identity supersedes personal identity. Although this conception can appear to protect Black lawyers against accusations of bias, he argues that people cannot abstract away their identities and that professional norms are not necessarily neutral.
qs: Once you become a lawyer, you adopt a professional identity that supersedes everything about you and you are governed entirely by a kind of professional ethic of what it means to be a lawyer, which is to abstract away who you are as a person.
But that conception is false, he added. Nobody is abstracted from who they are, and professional norms themselves are not always neutral or independent of identity.

kp.k: Integration and social justice impose distinct professional demands
kp.d: Wilkins interprets Brown v. Board of Education as promising both equality through integration and social justice through law. Expanded access does not itself ensure substantive change. Black lawyers inherit both commitments but face greater risks in pursuing social change because their credibility is already questioned; Wilkins nevertheless frames the relationship between lawyering and justice as a challenge for all lawyers.
qs: “On the one hand, *Brown* promises equality through integration, which implies that if we just provide equal access and opportunity, that’s all we’re obligated to do in order to produce a just society.”
But *Brown* also promises social justice through law, implying that lawyers should fight for equality and social change.
Just because you change the demographics of the people who are in power doesn’t mean that the power changes, he added.

“All lawyers face the challenge of what is it that is required of us by the relationship between lawyering and justice in a world that we know is riven by injustice. And we also know that the rule of law is more important today than it ever has been.”

kp.k: Legal education helped organize transformative litigation
kp.d: Wilkins presents Charles Hamilton Houston’s move from solo practice to leadership at Howard Law School as a mechanism connecting legal education to constitutional change. He credits Houston with creating the litigation campaign that eventually produced Brown v. Board of Education.
qs: After graduation, said Wilkins, he did what almost all Black lawyers of his generation did, working in solo practice.
But he eventually became the vice dean of Howard Law School, and from there created the litigation campaign that eventually resulted in the landmark decision of *Brown v. Board of Education*.

kp.k: Formal desegregation did not eliminate exclusion in legal education
kp.d: Wilkins distinguishes the end of de jure segregation from continuing de facto segregation in law and legal education. He illustrates persistent exclusion through his comparison of Harvard Law’s classes of 1965 and 1865, then describes a summer recruitment and preparation program for Black students from historically Black colleges and universities as an effort to desegregate legal education.
qs: “But although *Brown* signaled the end of de jure segregation,” Wilkins said, “first in the public schools and then, in a series of decisions, in other areas of American life, it did not end de facto segregation, including in the legal profession or legal education.”
Putting this in a Harvard context, Wilkins said the class of 1965 had the same number of Black lawyers as the class of 1865: one.
It brought together over the summer a group of talented Black seniors and juniors from historically Black colleges and universities to recruit and prepare them to apply and attend law school.
